pharm: Substance use disorder treatment - opioid/alcohol dependence
quick: 50 mg orally once daily (alcohol or opioid dependence)
With or without food; taking with food may reduce GI upset

summary: Naltrexone is a pure, long-acting opioid receptor antagonist used in the management of alcohol dependence and to block the effects of exogenous opioids. It has no opioid agonist activity. Patients must be opioid-free for a minimum of 7-10 days before starting to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Naltrexone carries a dose-related hepatotoxicity warning, so liver function should be monitored. It is effective only as part of a comprehensive treatment program.
indications: Blockade of the effects of exogenously administered opioids (as part of opioid dependence management)

dosage.n: Begin only after opioid-free interval of 7-10 days

dosage.d: e.g., 100 mg every other day or 150 mg every third day
dosage.n: Flexible regimens to improve adherence; same weekly total

admin: Confirm the patient is opioid-free for at least 7-10 days before the first dose
Consider a naloxone challenge test if opioid-free status is uncertain
Take with or without food; food may lessen nausea
Do not start while the patient is in acute opioid withdrawal
Provide as part of a structured addiction treatment program with counseling
moa: Naltrexone is a synthetic opioid antagonist that competitively binds to and blocks opioid receptors (predominantly mu), preventing exogenous opioids from producing their effects. In alcohol dependence it is thought to reduce the rewarding/reinforcing effects of alcohol via modulation of the endogenous opioid system, thereby reducing craving and heavy drinking.

absolute: Patients currently physically dependent on opioids (including methadone/buprenorphine)
Failed naloxone challenge test or positive urine opioid screen
relative: Anticipated need for opioid analgesia (e.g., upcoming surgery)

preg: There are limited human data. Naltrexone should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Discuss continuation versus discontinuation with the patient individually.
lact: Naltrexone and its metabolite are excreted in human milk. Because of potential effects on the breastfed infant, use with caution and weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the clinical need for the drug.
renal: Naltrexone and its major metabolite are excreted primarily in urine. Use with caution in renal impairment as clearance may be reduced; specific dose adjustments are not well established.
hepatic: Naltrexone has caused dose-related hepatocellular injury at doses higher than recommended. It is contraindicated in acute hepatitis or liver failure, and should be used cautiously with monitoring in patients with hepatic impairment or active liver disease.

major: Opioid-containing products (analgesics, antidiarrheals, antitussives) - blocked effect and risk of precipitated withdrawal; danger of opioid overdose if patient takes large doses to overcome blockade
moderate: Thioridazine (reports of lethargy and somnolence when combined)
Yohimbine (additive negative effects in some reports)
interactions.food: No significant food interaction; food may reduce GI upset
interactions.alcohol: Treats alcohol dependence; does not prevent alcohol intoxication or impairment
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor liver enzymes; may interfere with opioid-based pain management plans

serious: Opioid overdose due to attempts to override blockade or after loss of tolerance
emergency: Opioid overdose / respiratory depression after attempting to overcome blockade

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline and periodically
Confirmation of opioid-free status before initiation (history, urine screen, naloxone challenge)
Signs of opioid withdrawal at start of therapy
Adherence and engagement in the broader treatment program
counsel: You must be off all opioids for 7-10 days before starting, or you may get sudden, severe withdrawal
Do not use opioids to try to override the blockade - it can cause fatal overdose
Carry a card or alert noting you take naltrexone in case you need emergency pain treatment
Your tolerance to opioids drops - using opioids after stopping naltrexone can be deadly
Report yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine, or severe abdominal pain (liver warning)
This medicine works best combined with counseling and a support program
pk: Opioid blockade begins within about 1 hour of an oral dose
Plasma peak about 1 hour after oral administration
Blockade of 50 mg lasts roughly 24 hours; 100-150 mg lasts longer (48-72 h)
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Must be opioid-free 7-10 days before initiation to avoid precipitated withdrawal
A naloxone challenge can help confirm opioid-free status when in doubt
Dose-related hepatotoxicity - monitor LFTs and avoid in acute hepatitis/liver failure
Reduced opioid tolerance after stopping increases overdose risk if opioids are resumed
Effective only within a comprehensive treatment and counseling program
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule - do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Experience with naltrexone overdose in humans is limited; very high doses have caused liver toxicity. There is no specific antidote. Manage supportively with monitoring of liver function and vital signs; treat in a setting equipped for cardiopulmonary support.
